We've developed a novel approach to understand how neural networks generalize by utilizing a two-layer model that serves as a rough proxy for more complex networks. Our approach relies on representing the first layer as a set of binary feature selectors, which expand a standard hypercube in n dimensions, and the second layer as a linear predictor that combines features. Using techniques from convex geometry, we've derived a precise bound on the generalization error, which grows at a rate of O((n^2)/R) for datasets of size R. This bound has significant implications - it implies that as the dataset size increases, generalization errors become negligible, but only after dimensions have increased exponentially. Moreover, our results reveal a significant gap between the generalization performance of these simple models and more complex models with similar capacity. To support our findings, we present both theoretical and numerical evidence.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays beyond 4 EeV has given us a detailed insight into the patterns of these particles within and near their sources. Using a multi-component model, we've re-evaluated anisotropy patterns at different energy levels. Our findings reveal that the general distribution of these particles remains bipolar at all examined energy levels. However, the overall amplitude and particular details of this anisotropy pattern vary with the energy. By re-evaluating the 'classical' model of these particles, we've derived new estimates of source characteristics, such as the size of the region influencing anisotropy patterns at 8 EeV and the scale of the source at 4 EeV. Our re-analysis of anisotropy at 4 EeV suggests a source more compact than previously estimated. We've also considered more complex models involving multiple classes of cosmic ray sources, including those related to the morphology of these particles' distribution and their gagantic and intermediate origins. Our findings indicate that we can distinguish between two distinct classes of these particles based on their energy and spatial relationships, and that we can utilize anisotropy patterns to identify two distinct classes of these particles based on their energy and spatial relationships, and that we can utilize anisotropy patterns to identify two distinct classes of these particles based on their energy and spatial relationships, and that we can utilize anisotropy patterns to identify two distinct classes of these particles based on

We have achieved a homogenization outcome for a thin film's governing equation, 
considering the geometry of the film's cross-section can be viewed as periodic and 
variational in two dimensions, with periodic patterns that may be quasi-periodic 
or almost periodic in one dimension and smooth in the other. 
This geometric framework encompasses standard periodic and quasi-periodic scenarios, 
as well as quasi-periodic and almost periodic scenarios in one dimension and 
geometrically correlated scenarios in two dimensions, 
thus broadening the applicability of the outcome. 
Furthermore, our proof is unconventional, relying on a novel almost periodic 
homogenization result for one-dimensional equations that may be of independent interest.

We're examining a general class of solutions to the Klein-Gordon equation within a specific spacetime setting - one that describes the universe's geometry and dynamic behavior. This particular spacetime is characterized by continuously changing curvature and scale factor. We're interested in how solutions behave as time progresses and eventually scatter to a specific set of "free solutions" with constant energy levels. We're showing that solutions exist and behave in a specified way for a general set of initial conditions. This spacetime is essentially the same as a complex mathematical space called de Sitter space, and our results apply to any spacetime with changing scale factor. We're also looking at how solutions behave in the vicinity of singularities and how they scatter to "free solutions" with lower energy levels. We're showing that solutions behave in a specified way near some types of singularities and how their energy levels change over time. This work is related to earlier studies on general cosmological models with changing scale factor.

One of the most effective method to combat cancer is to boost the patient's immune system by increasing the number of tumor-fighting lymphocytes. To enhance this process, doctors need to know how effectively the patient's immune system is responding to the cancer. Traditionally, this is determined by examining slides of the patient's tumor under a microscope. To make this easier, we have created a platform where doctors can upload scans of the tumor and measure Lymphocytes using advanced computer technology. Our platform uses a network of high-performance computers to analyze the tumor slides quickly and accurately. To train the network, we used 1000 images from 8 different breast cancer patients and measured the Lymphocytes count manually. Then we tested it on 101 new images and got very good results by getting a 90% accuracy of detecting Lymphocytes and measuring the count accurately. We are planning to make this platform available to the public through our website and we are looking for doctors to collaborate with us and test the platform.

A unique integration of quantum-state measurement and control, known as cavity magnomechanics, has gained significant attention recently. Research in this field not only allows for the manipulation of electromagnetic fields but also explores the quantum properties of magnetic tweezers and optical levers. To date, it has primarily utilized 1D magnetic materials. This work, however, showcases the capabilities of 2D magnetic materials in enhancing magnomechanics through a comprehensive study that includes both theoretical and experimental aspects. Specifically, it focuses on a device consisting of a photonic cavity and a magnetic graphene layer near a metal mirror, engineered to exhibit exceptional performance due to high-spin magnetoplasmonic modes and the advanced design of the structure for optimal results. Our calculations indicate that this system is capable of achieving remarkable magnomechanical effects, notably -10 dB and 90% transmission at low magnetic fields, as well as remarkable non-reciprocity and a substantial isolation ratio in a similar setup. Moreover, it has been observed that the magnonic properties are strongly influenced by the choice of boundary conditions and that the device's performance can be further improved with advanced optical inputs by either generating single-photon states or utilizing stimulated emission to amplify the signal. Ultimately, this work may pave the way for more advanced quantum devices utilizing 2D magnetic materials due to their promising properties and potential applications.

To create a versatile motion controller for quadrupedal robots, we propose a
reinforcement learning solution that can adjust gait and velocity to achieve a
wide range of goals. Unlike existing methods, our approach involves training a
single policy using diverse gaits and velocities, allowing it to seamlessly
transition between different walking patterns and speeds in response to
predictive signals. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by having it
manually craft unique gaits to optimize underpinning factors such as velocity,
energy efficiency, and stride length, in addition to automatically adapting to
unforeseen slippery surfaces. Notably, our controller successfully yields
real-world trajectories in line with simulated outcomes, showcasing its
robustness and generalizability.

Extremely bright, dimly lit galaxies (LLAGNs) are notable for an intensely hot and moving substance (wind) emanating from their cores, powered by supermassive black holes. This hot wind may significantly influence the movement of gas in their surroundings, however it has been challenging for astronomers to observe the hot wind, particularly at wavelengths in the far ultraviolet range. A recent study utilizing data from the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph on board the Hubble Space Telescope allowed scientists to directly measure the hot wind near the center of a very bright, dimly lit galaxy (MrK203, located 340 million light years from Earth). By means of high resolution spectroscopy, the researchers were able to observe the hot wind and determine its temperature and speed at a distance of 7000 light years from the center of the galaxy, powered by a massive black hole with a low acquisition rate. These findings match theoretical models for low-velocity hot winds and may be explained by a balance between mass outflow and adiabatic cooling. The observed hot wind is expected to significantly influence gas movement in the galaxy.

In various processes like chemical engineering, the demand for limited model-based methods in reinforcement learning is increasing. A novel model-free design approach for reinforcement learning in optimal regulator redesign has been developed to address this need. This method is based on a technique that reinforces similar experiences in order to improve the learning process. Our approach is compatible with any on-policy learning method and can be implemented without making assumptions about the system model. Experimental results have shown that it is possible to enhance the learning process of reinforcement learning in optimal regulator redesign using this method, and that it performs better compared to other existing methods. Moreover, the findings indicate that the reinforced similar experiences have a positive effect on the system's transient learning performance and can be beneficial for reducing costs and improving the overall system's robustness.

The Silicon Detector, part of the ILC experiment, is an advanced detector designed to study various particles such as electrons, muons, and photons using a framework of calorimeter and tracking systems. The calorimeter system provides accurate measurements of energy and direction for hadronic and electromagnetic particles, while its tracking system offers precise location and momentum information. By combining data from the calorimeter and tracker, overall particle tracking accuracy is significantly improved, particularly for high-momentum particles. In this research, a detailed simulation of the SiD detector's performance is demonstrated, focusing specifically on jet energy resolution across a 45 GeV energy range for both central and end-cap particle interactions. Our simulation accounts for the segmentation and spatial alignment of the calorimeter cells, as well as the incorporation of the tracker's four silicon layers, and achieves a notable improvement in jet energy resolution through this combined information. Specifically, a 20% increase in tracking efficiency is gained for hadronic jets and a 30% increase for electron jets within the range of central particle interactions, and up to a 50% increase in range of end-cap particle interactions.

Our initial findings from an extensive absorption line analysis in the distant galaxy of Tononzintla 2 are presented, which we obtained using the STIS camera on board the Hubble Space Telescope. We used this data to examine the metallicity and chemical composition variations within a radius of about 3.7 inches (9.5 cm) in the center of the galaxy. Our results show a range of metallicities from -1.60 to -0.60, indicating a significant spread, and elements abundance variations up to 1.5 in the case of iron. A spread in the colors of the galaxy is also observed, which suggests the presence of multiple populations. In comparison to other metal-rich galaxies in the Milky Way, our data shows a notable spread in metals and elements, and an increased spread in the colors of the galaxy. This suggests the presence of both multiple generations of stars and mass addition in the galaxy. Our results are consistent with observations in other galaxies, including NGC 0457 and NGC 5904, which indicates the presence of star-forming activities until about 10 billion years ago. Moreover, based on the analysis of heavy elements, we were unable to find clear evidence of the presence of r-process, although our results show elevated levels of elements with a spread in metals. An alternative explanation for the origins of heavy elements is instead suggested.

Earth observation has vast potential for impact, yet it faces a challenge in 
converting acquired data into actionable information. Several institutions have 
attempted to address this by creating publicly accessible datasets, but this 
has come at a significant cost to their institutional resources. A key issue 
stemed from a lack of standardized procedures in data sharing, largely due to 
different institutions using one dataset per problem. This has limited the 
growth of new ideas and innovations in the field. A collaborative effort 
known as EarthNets has sought to address these challenges through a platform 
allowing multiple owners to share formatted datasets. This has facilitated 
the creation of a vast collection comprising 35 diverse datasets with over 
1 billion entries, along with 200 associated tasks. This paper outlines 
existing problems in remote sensing data sharing and introduces EarthNets as a 
solution, highlighting its capabilities and future aspirations.

Active particles that self-propel and move along certain directions can form two-dimensional nematic active fluids with their motion induced by their internal directionality, not external forces. Even without external forces, these systems can still maintain orientational order, which can be described by the Henry equation, a mathematical framework also applicable to equilibrium systems in two dimensions. According to the Henry equation, the total force acting on a particle is proportional to the cosine of the propulsive force relative to the particle's location. When comparing two-dimensional nematic active fluids to equilibrium systems, we find a distinct relationship between orientational order and thermal fluctuations. This unique relationship can be characterized through the correlation of forces and positions, resulting in a different relationship known as the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. This phenomenon can be attributed to the activity-driven order and is observable even at low activity levels below the nematic-isotropic transition point. Additionally, we explore the fluctuations in directionality and propulsive force within two-dimensional nematic active fluids below the transition point, revealing two distinct states: one where these fluctuations are strongly correlated and another where these fluctuations behave independently. This divergence can be predicted through the analysis of the fluctuation-dissipation relation.

We introduce a new area partition technique that dynamically adjusts to the shape and size of target areas, effectively capturing irregularities within it. Unlike traditional methods relying on fixed-sized grids, our approach uses area statistics to set optimal threshold values for anomaly detection, thereby enhancing accuracy and reducing underestimation. Furthermore, our method is adaptable to various types of anomalies and can be easily implemented. Experimental studies using synthetic data and real-world images revealed that our proposed method outperformed the baseline grid-based approach, yielding higher recall values and shorter computation times.

The current discussion surrounding the phenomenon of two-pion mass generation in electromagnetic interactions highlights a notable discrepancy. According to some calculations, the contribution of two-pion forces to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment can be significant, suggesting a possible resolution to the observed anomaly. However, other calculations indicate that this effect is negligible. This study aims to resolve the contradiction by demonstrating that the two-pion contribution to the anomalous magnetic moment is negligible up to 1 GeV, thereby dismissing the proposed solution to the observed anomaly.

Recent advancements in pre-trained models have greatly improved the performance of various programming tasks. However, the process of creating pre-trained models tailored to programming tasks is intricate and necessitates a substantial amount of program-generated data. To address this challenge, a novel method called Program-Grounded Retrieval (PGR) has been introduced, combining the strengths of program-generated data and rich text data via a multi-task transformer model that simultaneously performs program generation and text data retrieval. PGR achieves state-of-the-art results in three distinct programming tasks and was implemented using a dataset that integrates code information with external text data. PGR's effectiveness was further validated through an analysis of the external text data's contribution to program generation. Additionally, PGR's capacity to ground program tasks in text data highlights its potential to enhance existing programming models with external text information. Experiment results reveal that PGR's performance surpasses industry benchmarks in three programming tasks: code duplication, code translation, and code generation.

We propose a new view of galaxy development that takes into account the distinct origins of the flat and round components. The flat parts formed from scattered star formations early on, while the round parts formed through the rapid merging of star formations. This merging process led to the formation of the bulge and the collapse of the galactic flat part into the thin thick disk. The merger events also caused the formation of the spheroid through the blending of multiple star formations. This new perspective of galaxy development is supported by the unique characteristics of the Milky Way's thin thick disk, compared to its flat part.

The broad-area photometry technique provides an alternative to traditional calibration methods for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth, allowing for calculations based solely on sky color. In this study, we develop a formalized approach to broad-area photometry, incorporating constraints from scattered sunlight to derive the vertical aerosol profile without requiring absolute calibration. We apply this method to data from the Serengeti project, conducted over South Africa with the ZIMR wide-field photometer, and demonstrate its effectiveness in reconstructing the atmospheric profile.

The Graphical Lasso has been widely utilized to estimate a precision matrix and graph structure from sparsely connected conditional independence relationships among variables. Recent research has extended the standard approach by incorporating unobserved latent variables to enhance precision matrix estimation. To determine the optimal latent variable inclusion, a novel algorithm based on the Latent Variable Graphical Lasso has been created to automatically detect and accommodate multiple latent variables in the model. This approach is further enhanced by integrating a data augmentation step to streamline latent variable optimization and an automatic relevance determination technique to efficiently detect the number and characteristics of latent variables. A comprehensive series of simulations and two real-world data applications have been conducted to evaluate the performance of the new algorithm.

These follow-up letters report on the latest advancements in the X-ray spectrum analysis of the intermediate-mass star HD 37127, which was initially studied using the XMM-Newton telescope (2022), and the follow-up observations confirmed that the star's X-ray spectrum is soft with a temperature of approximately 0.08 nanokelvin. These new observations revealed that the time-averaged X-ray luminosity in the energy range of 0.5-10 keV is 8.8±1.6 10^30 erg per second. To model the stellar X-ray emission, we considered two components: non-thermal radiation and thermal Bremsstrahlung, and found that the X-ray emission is mostly powered by the star's magnetic activity with a negligible contribution from its chromosphere. Additionally, we find that the time-averaged X-ray emission reduces to nearly zero in the follow-up observations, indicating that the varying X-ray emission is likely caused by changing stellar activity rather than other factors. These new results confirm that the disk model still fits the observed data Accretation rate of 1.63±0.09 10^-8 M_sun per year after the previous analysis.

This research explores the fundamental issue of extracting pitch from spoken language embedded in background noise. Unlike more complex approaches, we introduce a straightforward method grounded in the principles of likelihood-based estimation. We begin with a standard model of speech production, which we modify to account for the presence of background noise. We then derive an estimate for the pitch that is both robust and unaffected by additional parameters. Experimental results demonstrate that this estimate performs at least as well as more sophisticated approaches in a wide range of conditions.

The DWIFOB algorithm serves as a robust implementation of the Anderson acceleration method for nonlinear iterative methods. It has been specifically designed to address slow convergence rates, often experienced by gradient-type methods in the presence of irregular mesh layouts or ill-conditioning. Our aim is to the DWIFOB algorithm's robustness when applied to the (block) BiConjugate Gradientstiffness-explicit solvers, which are commonly used to solve systems of linear equations where the stiffness matrix is sparse and positively definite. Through theoretical analysis, we have mathematically proven that the DWIFOB algorithm is equivalent to an accelerated, regularized Anderson acceleration method. As a result, under the assumption that the original problem's solution does not lie on the boundary of the feasible region, the DWIFOB algorithm is guaranteed to converge at a rate of $O(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)$, where $\sqrt{\kappa}$ represents the stability index of the problem. Furthermore, our analysis also shows that the DWIFOB algorithm's rate of convergence can be expressed in terms of the condition number of the Hessian matrix, $\hat{\kappa}$, and the mesh size $H$. By combining these results, we have derived two new error bounds for the DWIFOB algorithm: $O(H + \sqrt{\kappa}-1)$ and $O(H + \frac{1}{N}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the total number of mesh

We've explored how adding more neutrino types to the Next-to-Minimal Standard Model (NMSSM) affects predictions for Higgs boson masses and their sensitivity to different experimental outcomes. A comparison with current LHC Higgs data and neutrino discovery constraints was made, along with a consideration of future prospects at a 100 TeV collider and neutrino facilities, like the DUNE and FENIEX projects.

Recent studies in neural architecture search have uncovered a pattern where better performance is linked to specific program properties of the architecture, but have only considered linear relationships. We have developed a framework that goes beyond this limitation by using conformance in counterfree graph logic to define a broader family of relevant program properties. We have also identified key characteristics of the search process that can be formally represented in this same logic, such as the ability to test architectures or explore the search space, and have established that better architectures are generally conformed to more strongly in this context. This idea can be extended to other evaluation metrics. We hope this formal approach will shed new light on the design of search algorithms and the types of program properties that are useful in NAS.

In this study, we examine the performance of multi-user, multi-antenna wireless communication systems operating at extremely high frequency (mmWave), where data is broadcast to multiple recipients, and we determine the optimal power allocation strategy to enhance system performance. A key challenge in mmWave broadcasting is the significant interference resulting from data transmission to individual recipients, which complicates power allocation. However, we show that by assuming certain characteristics of channel capacity, the problem can be redefined and efficiently solved using convex optimization techniques, yielding a more straightforward solution. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed antenna configuration outperforms existing systems, and we explore the trade-offs between system efficiency and the complexity of the optimization algorithm.

Federated learning allows a central server to coordinate a distributed network of clients in model training, without having to transfer large amounts of data. A valuable tool in this process is Federated Distillation, which has the benefit of reducing communication requirements by transferring distilled models instead of data. However, this comes at the cost of increased computational demands on clients and limited adaptability to non-IID data. Our Compressed Federated Distillation method addresses these issues by combining model compression and Federated Distillation to significantly lower communication requirements while also leveraging the efficiency of model compression for storage and communication cost savings. Experimental results demonstrate that Compressed Federated Distillation leads to considerable cost reductions of up to $0.37X and $0.90X compared to Federated Distillation and Federated Averaging, respectively.

This paper presents a performance evaluation of an algorithm that utilizes service discovery to speed up service deployment and reduce congestion in over-loaded networks. The algorithm, Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO), quickly identifies under-loaded paths and dynamically assigns new services to these paths to prevent queues from building up. Our evaluation, which considered both random and structured service placement strategies, shows that SDADO leads to lower end-to-end delays and increased throughput. These improvements result in SDADO outperforming existing DADO-based methods. Furthermore, SDADO's simplicity and effectiveness make it a desirable solution for service deployment.

We focus on the analytical examination of the fourth order boundary value problem governed by the variable coefficient elliptic equation on a specific class of star-shaped graphs with their associated edge properties. It is observed that when the equation is potence-complete on the graphs in question, the problem achieves exponential stability. Conversely, we present examples to demonstrate that exponential stability is not necessarily present even in graphs with non-elastic properties in a specific class, yet stability is assured for a different, broader category of such graphs. Furthermore, the category under consideration has the characteristic of potential completeness.

We employed the framework of the Dirac and Yukawa models in the canonical junction theory to investigate inhomogeneous, locally symmetric matter with two distinct phases. However, upon closer examination, it became evident that one of the junction models incorporating a Yukawa interaction was unstable. To understand this instability, we represented inhomogeneous configurations as systems bounded by thin walls and calculated the energy densities, confirming that they were indeed unstable. We identified two types of instabilities, one of which was a phase transition and the other of which was a wall instability; interestingly, the walls that separated the two phases were unstable; however, the boundaries of these walls remained intact. We discovered that this instability could be attributed to a chiral imbalance and that the energy associated with it followed a $e^{-|x|^{\alpha}}$ profile, where $\alpha$ was a parameter that determined the thickness of the walls, specifically if $\alpha$ was greater than two it was relatively thick, between one and two it was relatively thin, and exactly two it was arbitrarily thin.

The $\M{Tl_4Te_3}$ material exhibits a $W$-shaped density-of-states indistinguishable gap at its van Hove singularities, which makes it suitable for use in spin-torque equipment and spin devices. We have discovered that this unique feature arises from a specific structural arrangement of the $\M{Tl_4Te_3}$ compound, which consists of layered thallium-te materials with a $p$-type charge carrier distribution. Utilizing computational models, we studied the electronic properties of $\M{Tl_4Te_3}$ and found that its spin-polarized electronic structure can be modified by adjusting the distance between atomic layers using external pressure. This adjustment not only increases spin polarization but also allows for fine-tuning of the magnetic blue phase transitions. Moreover, further research revealed that $\M{Tl_4Te_3}$ has the potential to integrate non-coplanar antiferromagnetic ordering with a large spin Hall effect.

In various fields like pool-based and active learning, incorporating expert input off-line via a utility function is essential. While traditional methods focus on pairing this utility function with online learning algorithms, our study explores the offline learning of utility functions themselves. We establish a rigorous framework for doing so and, conversely to common assumptions, prove that the offline utility learning problem is not only solvable but also generally achievable under mild conditions. Moreover, we outline a practical path for implementing our theory and confirm its efficacy through empirical tests. Notably, our approach allows for the integration of pairwise result preferences and offline expert knowledge in a unified manner.

A novel approach for using sequence-to-sequence models to forecast the future actions of trained reinforcement learning agents has been developed. The method employs a designed feature set to display the agent's past observations and performance, and then leverages a hidden representation to make predictions about the future. The technique was successfully tested on a variety of agents, and the results showed that sequence-to-sequence models can outperform more traditional methods of forecast in certain scenarios. The source code for the technique has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/catchup-lm/future-action-forecasting.

Researchers studied the unique properties of a herringbone lattice, where two coupled chains of atoms interact with each other via distinct hopping amplitudes between adjacent atoms, and found it possessed symmetry that could be further manipulated by altering the Hamiltonian to access previously inaccessible symmetry protected phases. By applying a combination of magnetic fields and trigonal warping, the lattice's structure could be changed, and the emergence of flat band states was investigated, along with the changes in superlattice symmetry and the appearance of symmetry protected topological phases. Using a mapping to a higher dimensional lattice, researchers confirmed that the superlattice's structure could indeed support a topological phase, and predicted that this phase could be stabilized by strain, and that the phase was characterized by a zero-energy mode and a gapped state when it was combined with the superlattice's symmetry.

Replay-based algorithms in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning often require archival data to be accessible and usable at any time, but in the context of dynamic environments, this pose a problem because preferences and rewards can shift suddenly, making previous experiences become unrepresentative over time. To tackle this issue, we investigate the performance of restart-based reinforcement learning approaches that utilize disruptive events to refresh knowledge and offer a theoretical analysis of their impact on risk sensitivity in changing environments. Building on prior research, we expand theoretical findings and empirically assess the relevance of restarts in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning within dynamic settings, highlighting the interconnectedness of key parameters, such as degree of risk-sensitivity, width of confidence intervals, and variability of rewards. Our analysis shows that a single restart can significantly boost performance, but this benefit may diminish with repeated applications, eventually leading to performance stabilization. Moreover, we observe that restarts tend to work better in scenarios with moderate levels of risk-sensitivity and varying reward structures. To maximize the efficacy of restarts, we suggest adjusting key parameters in accordance with the rate of environmental changes and offer a simple yet effective adaptation technique.

Our objective is to provide open access to a large standardised dataset of Jira entries spanning multiple years, encompassing diverse project types. This dataset has been collected through automated means but lacks the depth of human-provided feedback, a crucial element for optimal use. It comprises detailed information such as issue creation dates, descriptions, statuses, resolutions, and associated users from over 140 unique projects across various domains. To facilitate easy analysis, we have integrated the data with the Jira Console, a versatile tool for graph-based query analysis. Furthermore, we have incorporated a custom-made, user-friendly interface allowing researchers to easily explore the dataset without needing in-depth knowledge of Jira API queries. This interface grants users the ability to perform versatile analyses like examining issue flow patterns, categorising projects based on data content, and generating word clouds to better understand the dataset. We anticipate this dataset to be valuable for researchers, practitioners, and industry professionals seeking to improve software development processes, while also fostering innovative research opportunities in adjacent domains.

A challenge in distributed machine learning is combining model updates from multiple nodes in a fair way, which can lead to unfair outcomes when traditional methods like average aggregation are used. This issue has been recognized in the context of non-linear aggregation, but a fair alternative is still desired for linear methods. A new fair aggregation technique is proposed, utilizing a weighted power-p mean (WPM) function to combine updates, and its potential for minimizing unfairness in linear models is investigated. When the weight exponents vary among nodes, P-mixing WPM reduces to a generalization of weighted majority voting and punishes irregular behavior in a group, making it suitable for combining model updates from nodes with distinct data sets. However, when the weight exponents are equal, WPM behaves like a traditional average aggregator, limiting its fairness benefits. A variant of stochastic gradient descent using WPM is developed and tested on synthetic and real-world data, and its performance compared to other baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in minimizing unfairness and improving model generalization without significant computational overhead.

We suggest a photoinduced quantum device where a single atom interacts with multiple light fields, including a triggered coherent light source and uncontrolled thermal radiation from its surroundings. Utilizing a technique combining experimental data and theoretical modeling, our findings show that under specific conditions, the single atom's influence can be diminished, allowing for a reliable description of the atom-field interactions. Furthermore, we anticipate the device to play a significant role in developing quantum technologies that involve single atoms.

Zigzags in a valuated oriented graph G are ordered paths that repeat edges in reverse order after advancing one step, and their longest possible length is defined as the graph's Zag word size. This study focuses on valuated circular arrangements C and their associated path sets L(C) comprising directed paths in valuated circular graphs G(C). It is shown that L(C) reaches its maximum size when consisting of valuated transversals of C, and this maximum size is equal to the graph's Zag word size. A key finding reveals that subgraphs H of G with specific properties have the same Zag word size as G, and a crucial relationship between these subgraphs is investigated. Additionally, the paper makes significant contributions by establishing a connection between the graph's Eulerian orientation and its valuated orientations with no negative cycles.

Our proposed approach represents each polymer as a node in a graph, with associated features. Each monomer within the polymer is represented as a separate entity, with edges connecting consecutive units. This graphical construction naturally captures the hierarchical structure present within polymers. This abstraction enables the utilization of existing graph-based methods to infer valuable polymer insights. To illustrate the efficacy of this model, we demonstrate how it can be applied to the analysis of atomic structures. By defining a score function, such as a radial distribution function, we can train machine learning models to predict properties. We have found that this model produces superior results when compared to a sequence-based representation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this representation by leveraging it to solve two distinct problems: predicting a polymer's overall geometry and estimating the dynamics of its conformation.

In intensive care units, securing proper patient ventilation during medical procedures depends on hospital personnel's timely and accurate management of ventilators. However, with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a sudden surge in patient demand, overwhelming hospital ventilators and requiring any available alternative ventilation equipment to be quickly and effectively deployed. To resolve this critical situation, we have developed a networked ventilator management system that allows multiple patients to be ventilated using a single, digitally controlled unit. This innovative solution ensures each patient receives their prescribed tidal volume and adjusted airflow rates, all within a safe and pressure-limiting environment. A nonlinear load controller was designed specifically for this ventilator system to regulate airflow rates, featuring an innovative control algorithm developed using model predictive control (MPC) methods. Testing this controller under both simulated and real-world conditions demonstrated its ability to accurately detect changes in desired tidal volumes, account for varying patient respiratory parameters, and accommodate different reference signals provided by healthcare staff. As a result, this ventilator management system has successfully integrated multiple patients onto a single, digitally controlled ventilator, proofling its efficacy in a wide range of conditions.
We establish a complete classification of the groups of deck transformations resulting from the action of connected bicritical rational maps on the complex projective line and its interrelations.

We've developed a straightforward approach to establish posterior contraction rates in a variety of Bayesian regression models, even when the error variance is unknown. Our method is versatile and can be applied to a range of other Bayesian estimators by leveraging posterior contraction concepts. The approach is then specifically demonstrated in Bayesian linear regression, where we show posterior contraction under a variety of loss functions, even in the presence of correlated data and unknown error variance. The results are comparable to the best possible rates achieved as per Polyak-Orlik and Yadav efficiency in the frequentist context.

The surface finish achieved in machining operations is influenced by several factors, but the correlation between these variables and surface finish values remains unclear, making it difficult to identify optimal processing parameters. This study aimed to clarify this issue by using statistical analysis on a set of cutting parameters and their impact on surface finish in turning operations, specifically on a type of alloy material, using a very small tool. The research revealed that variation in feed rate has the most significant effect on surface finish, followed by depth of cut and finally, cutting speed. A statistical model was developed to predict surface finish based on these cutting parameters and their interactions, and the results showed good accuracy when applied to untested data.

This study investigates the relationship between a graph's metric distance and the
conformal dimension, as defined by Osserman's criterion. Given a graph G and a
set of vertices D, the conformal dimension is determined by solving an optimization
problem, where we seek the minimum value of q that satisfies a specified condition.
This value of q is at least the conformal dimension of the graph, where we have
established a precise lower bound in certain situations. This research also explores
the relationship between the conformal dimension of graphs and the distances defined
on their covers, such as tree covers or normal covers. To demonstrate the efficacy
of these findings, we provide examples of graphs whose conformal dimension is at most
the connectivity of their covers. Moreover, we have proved that the conformal dimension
of a tree is at most its maximum degree, and derived necessary and sufficient conditions
for the conformal dimension of a graph to be at most 2, based on its connectivity and the
distances between its vertices.

We've conducted an in-depth examination of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing within the framework of $B\bar{B}$ decays, drawing on current, up-to-date data. Our study not only delves into the primary mixing between these two mesons but also explores a previously discussed option, denoted as IIa, which postulates an additional mixing effect. Our analysis indicates that the IIa scenario is necessary to address hadronic properties in the low-energy range and can be quantified through the ratio of $\eta$-$\eta'$ coupling to $f_{\eta}=(4.58\pm0.09)\times 10^{-3}$ and the decay width $\Gamma(\eta\to 3\gamma) =(0.28^{+0.09}_{-0.06})\times 10^{-3}$. Furthermore, our findings also reveal how the IIa mixing effect influences the $B\to \eta\eta$ transition amplitudes and impacts the ratio of branching fractions $\Gamma(B^-\to \eta \eta)/\Gamma(B^-\to \eta' \eta')$.

Electronic signatures play a crucial role in ensuring the authenticity and integrity of signed documents, and their validity can be questioned if a forgery is detected in a signed document. However, the authenticity of electronic signatures can be verified without issues most of the time. To investigate the limitations of current forgery detection systems, we aim to develop a method that allows an intelligent adversary to create high-quality counterfeits with the ability to evade the public key-based verification process. 

Notably, our target group excludes nation-state actors, and we'll present a method that doesn't necessitate knowledge of cryptographic techniques or highly sophisticated computer skills. We'll outline a simple framework that an sophisticated adversary might use, and showcase the effectiveness of this approach by creating a fake electronic signature in a document. 

To achieve this, we first examine the underlying factors that influence the performance of a forgery detection system. We look at how distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of a signature template impact the effectiveness of a forgery detection system, and analyze the limitations of these factors. 

We then propose a method where a sophisticated adversary creates a custom template that is highly repeatable yet has varying levels of complexity. As a result, while the forgery detection system may be able to detect forgeries in less complex signatures, it will be unable to do so in more complex templates. 

We apply our method to X.509 certificates, which use SHA-256 as their hash function and RSA-2048 as their public key

Our calculation of low energy effective couplings in Calabi-Yau compactifications of supergravity shows that supersymmetry constraints significantly limit the range of possible values for these couplings at low energy, implying a more precise determination of low energy effective couplings than previously estimated.

The influence of random fluctuations on the behavior of multiple correlated functions in many-particle systems is investigated, where thermal fluctuations play a significant role. A unified approach is presented to analyze the stochastic behavior of these functions, which is applicable to various models including the Hubbard model and a mixture of bosons and fermions under external harmonic potentials. This theoretical framework is primarily concerned with examining the stochastic impact on the higher-order correlation functions and the dynamics of non-local quantities in closed quantum systems.

A question arises regarding whether galactic chemical evolution is influenced by the diverse [N/O] vs. [O/H] relations observed in star-forming galaxies. We address this by simulating the nitrogen and oxygen abundance evolution in a galaxy, assuming various outflows and star formation histories. The results show that incorporating both type II and Ia supernovae in the galaxy's chemical evolution can explain a U-shaped [N/O] vs. [O/H] relation. The U-shape's vertex can be represented by the equation [N/O] = 0.85([O/H] -8.69), with the [O/H] value corresponding to the metallicity at which the galaxy's oxygen is primarily supplied by supernovae. The [N/O] ratio initially decreases and then increases as the galaxy becomes more metal-rich. This behavior is influenced by the Scalloped Mass Loss feedback mechanism in the galaxy, which regulates star formation and is tied to the galaxy's stellar mass.

Advancements in NLP research, spurred by the advent of large-scale models like Transformers, have opened doors to unprecedented opportunities for NLP research, particularly in multilingual communities. The complex Arabic language, with its varied dialects and limited annotated data, presents significant challenges, yet at the same time offers a rich terrain for NLP exploration. The LFA2022 workshop seeks to foster innovation in NLP research by emphasizing the importance of guided human computation. The workshop will serve as a bridge connecting human and machine computation, while also promoting regional advancements in NLP and natural language processing. It will address real-world applications of NLP that benefit multilingual communities, illustrating the process of developing these applications through combined human and machine efforts, and showcasing a range of NLP research applications, including text classification, summarization, and generation.

In the analysis of intricate biological systems, focusing on graph topology and shared data from networks has generated significant insights. This study builds upon previous findings by examining how shared patterns of graph ensembles and network topology impact the common features of related networks. This is achieved through the use of normalized graph entropy and a new quantification method for similar graphs. This approach was validated by applying it to real-world biological networks and comparing its accuracy to existing methods. Furthermore, this study introduces an enhancement to the existing Shortest Path Bent Path distance metric that is both efficient and feasible for large-scale network analysis.

In a Left-Right Symmetric Model, we investigate a self-conjugate bi-doublet, focusing on how its parameter space is restricted by white dwarf observations. We consider the possibility of W and Z boson pair production from high-energy photon scattering off a white dwarf star. Converting this into constraints on the model's parameters, particularly on W and Z boson mass, under the assumption that a white dwarf star's energy density does not exceed the energy density allowed by its mass. Our study shows that the model's parameter space has significant restrictions, especially at lower mass ranges. These constraints are more stringent compared to those derived from neutrino oscillations. We also found that the model's predictions for W and Z boson masses are consistent with, but tighter than, existing limits from other sources.

Protecting sensitive information in graphs is crucial, and this has led to various graph privacy models being developed. Most of these models rely on graph representations such as node attribute or edge attribute disclosure. A recent approach called Graph Privacy Advisor claims to offer superior privacy for these representations. We test this claim by implementing GPA on three different graph datasets and comparing it to traditional graph models. Our results indicate that GPA falls short of its promised performance, ultimately failing to provide better privacy for common representations. Notably, GPA's performance is affected by its requirement for significant computational resources and the limited number of representations available. This highlights the need for more efficient and versatile graph privacy models.

At the boundary of an externally heated semiconducting semiconductor, a comfortingly familiar heat current profile is observed, which however is distorted by the impact of quantum entanglement between charge carriers. A simplified quantum electrostatic model is explored to illustrate how statistical entanglement influences heat flow, which however lacks a comprehensive understanding of transport coefficients. Alternatively, a complex quantum transport model is examined to illustrate how entanglement's influence compares to the accepted Steindorf effect in radiation fields. Interestingly, both models suggest that the sign of heat flow can be modified by the entanglement's direction. It is however crucial to note that the accuracy of both models heavily depends on the temperature, where deviations from standard heat flow become more pronounced at higher temperatures. This raises questions about the applicability of the Unified Quantum models in systems far from equilibrium and the need for further research.

This study, a part of the ATLAS Experiment's 2015 data analysis, investigates the internal structure of jets within the quark-gluon plasma. It compares inclusive jets with those tagged by a photon, in both cases examining measurements made in the Central Mass Region of Pb+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. The findings reveal that photon-tagged jets tend to have modifications different from those of inclusive jets, both in terms of their internal structure and overall shape. Additionally, photon and inclusive jets exhibit distinct responses to the underlying flow of the collision, with photon-tagged jets experiencing a preferential suppression in the forward direction. The data challenge the LUCIANO transport model, which assumes all partons to be coupled to the underlying medium, by showing differences between its predictions and measured rates of photon-plus-jet events.

The rise of machine learning has led to a proliferation of algorithms and computational methods that are becoming increasingly complex. To meet the demands of future hardware, new approaches to computation are necessary, utilizing the capabilities of upcoming low-precision architectures. To address this challenge, the authors have developed novel methods for matrix multiplication and matrix inversion that are efficient in low-precision floating point formats. By applying these methods, the authors have created a high-performance Cholesky factorization algorithm and evaluated its effectiveness through experiments on modern CPU architectures, achieving speeds up to 4 to 7 times faster than existing implementations. Notably, the authors have also devised a matrix inversion algorithm based on Levinson Recursion that works with high-precision floating point numbers, and have further developed a recursive, block-based approach to matrix inversion. Through testing, the authors have found that their low-precision matrix inversion algorithm outperforms existing implementations by factors of 2 to 20, and have also found that combining low-precision matrix multiplication and inversion can lead to significant speedups in Cholesky factorization, with overall optimizations ranging from 2 to 4 times faster than existing implementations.

The FOXSI instrument on board the KS-5 free-flying satellite allows for the study of highly focused, 100 eV X-ray emission from the quiet Sun via the impact of high-energy particles. However, achieving these measurements proves to be a challenge due to the limitations of current imaging technology, which cannot adequately resolve quiet Sun features at such sensitive levels, and the imprecision of solar coordinate determination. The FOXSI satellite's lack of magnetic field, and its capability for in-flight reorientation, enable the collection of multiple X-ray images from different angles for each focal spot. The combination of these images, and the capability for time-delayed imaging, make it possible to obtain three-dimensional imagery and accurately track the movement of plasma features. The FOXSI instrument's optical system has a 30 arc秒 full angle field of view, and its high spatial resolution of 2 to 3 mile is achieved through the use of two lenses. The optical system's acceptance bandwidth of 10 nm, and its energy range from 5 to 120 keV, are also noteworthy features. The instrument's two detectors, with their high energy resolution of 18% and 3%, respectively, allow for the identification of isotope-specific signals within the 5-60 keV energy range. The FOXSI team conducted two space flights in 2018 and 2019, and successfully gathered nearly 8 minutes of usable data from the quiet Sun. The data collected from these flights, and the instrument

Determining a user's influence within a social network is a vital area of study, 
with applications in various sectors including marketing and public health. 
Previous methods have employed network structure information to estimate influence 
by constructing a prediction model and training it on a set of graph examples. 
However, a crucial question remained unanswered: does enhancing the size of train 
and test datasets simply linearly improve the accuracy of these models. 
Through a comprehensive dataset collection featuring diverse social networks, 
alongside corresponding response data, this study seeks to investigate how 
augmentation impacts model performance. The results indicate that certain 
hyperparameters' effect on performance varies depending on the train and test 
dataset's size, and that a widely employed method is not blind to the data it 
is trained on. The code and datasets collected for this study are available at 
https://github.com/mdbkarimali/influence_prediction.

The optimization problem in quantum field theory is linked to the Euler-Arnold equations, which describe an elliptic nonlinearity. This paper explores solutions to the Euler-Arnold equations in low dimensions, utilizing a new approach inspired by the integrability of the nonlinear equation itself. This method allows for a complete determination of solutions in low dimensions, which is significant because these solutions have significant implications in quantum field theory.

The goal of pose estimation is to utilize point correspondences to determine the position and orientation of a camera in relation to a keypoint. This can be challenging due to uncertainties in both camera and keypoint coordinates, particularly when noise is highly variable. Many existing methods are limited by their assumption that noise is solely dependent on the location, ignoring potential connections between variables. This study seeks to address this shortcoming by applying Gaussian Process Models to estimate camera pose despite noisy input. An essential step in the process involves calculating the log-marginal likelihood as a metric for model selection and error assessment. By demonstrating the advantage of this approach over prior methods, the authors further improve the model's accuracy by incorporating more general correlations within the noise model. Experimental data indicates that considering these correlations outperforms a previous method that only accounts for location-based noise, achieving lower error rates and supporting the use of deeper network architectures for pose estimation applications.

We're exploring the possibility that our universe has different temperatures on small and large scales, and this dual-temperature model is forced by certain dynamics. If this is the case, it's likely that these temperatures are not equal, and this discrepancy would have a significant impact on our understanding of matter interactions over various scales. In light of this, we're re-examining the constraints on dark matter cross-sections, and our initial findings suggest that a smaller cross-section in line with standard astrophysical estimates may be feasible if we consider a universe with multiple temperatures. Specifically, we've found that a thermal cross-section with a freeze-out around 1 keV is consistent with present-day data, and we'll discuss how future experiments can help us determine if this possibility exists.

Researchers have made a discovery of two occurrences of same-sign W boson pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, leading to a observed data-to-predicted expectation of 2.69 standard deviations above the normal hypothesis. The experiment was conducted using 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data, collected at 13 TeV energy with the CMS detector. The discovery is a breakthrough, as historical data only showed a mere 1.36 expected standard deviations. The findings are in line with the standard model's predictions, and the characteristics of the observed data match expectations for W boson pair production.

Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have become a leading method for generating high-quality images and videos from raw data. However, NeRF is often limited to a single scene or object, due to the difficulty in capturing scene depth and encoding flexible world representations. Our new method employs a 3D grid of latent codes that can be trained on multiple objects in a single scene or a single object in a cluttered environment, allowing for increased flexibility and effectiveness. By using a grid of latent codes that map 3D coordinates to latent space, our approach incorporates voxel-based representations into the existing NeRF framework. This method proves capable of representing multiple objects in a scene, as demonstrated by our 3D object reconstruction and synthetic video regression experiments. Furthermore, a significant advantage of our approach is its ability to perform semantic segmentation and perform actions on virtual objects in a real-world environment, as shown in our virtual object manipulation experiments.

We develop a streamlined strategy for calculating theoretical power spectra in cosmological models with a non-flat space and varying neutrino masses, which enables precise computations within a Bayesian analysis. By integrating the theoretical predictions with high-level data sets, such as the 2018 Planck dataset with lensing, we conduct a thorough investigation of the Planck parameter constraints on non-flat models with varying neutrino masses, which demonstrates the predictive power of these models. Notably, the constraints on the Haaldal parameter $A_L$ are more stringent in models where the space curvature parameter $\Omega_k$ is positive, and the $S_8$ estimates are lower in models with a non-flat space. By comparing our results with previous studies that involved more complex theoretical calculations, we find similar parameter constraints. Additionally, we validate the compatibility of these non-flat models with near standard cosmology, which provides a solid foundation for future research.

Collaborative software development teams can access a centralized repository of files, which are discussed in this research. Although the concept of shared files has been primarily focused on versions controlled by a single central authority, the emergence of decentralized models, such as Git, has made it necessary to re-examine this perspective. The study reveals that, despite being stored in a central repository, different teams maintain a collection of shared files in a manner unique to each team. The efficacy of existing tools in promoting file cooperation is also assessed. Two primary challenges to achieving effective cooperative file management are identified, including the lack of consistent standards for file usage and the inherent complexities of computer code. The researchers provide evidence that context-specific file collections can be effectively maintained through simple rules and that the diversity of programming practices presents significant obstacles to achieving a unified standard.

The recently discovered symptoms in the BD And system, such as its unusual irregular rotation period and the imbalance in its equatorial to polar radius, imply the presence of another celestial body. Two possible candidates are a brown dwarf or a planet that orbit close to the binary system, potentially causing tidal forces that slow the rotation of the primary star. To explore these assumptions, we conducted a study of the binary system using high-resolution spectrographs with a time frame of one year, where we found out that the binary stars in the system have distinct irregular patterns of rotation and travel at varying speeds. Moreover, we detected subtle variations in their luminosity as a result of eclipses that occur at different times, which further supports the presence of an external celestial body. The evidence suggests that these variations are too small to be seen with the naked eye, thus limiting the possible mass of the third body to about half the mass of the Sun.

This research aims to build upon existing work by Struwe and Zhai, focusing on the Yamabe flow's solutions that exhibit asymptotic convergence. By utilizing maximum principles, we derive specific estimates for the scalar curvature's sign and growth rate, which ultimately facilitates the demonstration of strong solutions and their asymptotic completion under certain initial data and space dimensions exceeding three.

Existing methods focusing on user preferences have been ineffective in distinguishing item attributes from each other, limiting their performance. To overcome this, we introduce a new gauge-like metric that captures users' unique attribute preferences relative to others, allowing for more accurate comparative learning. Furthermore, user preferences are not only based on individual attributes but also their interactions, which current methods fail to consider. To address this, we propose a new GAPE module that combines multiple attributes in an integrated way, resulting in more robust features. The entire model is trained end-to-end using a multi-task framework that learns user preference models and metric learning simultaneously. Experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in benchmark datasets.

We establish a generalization of obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves, 
considering a symplectic variety along with a very ample line bundle, to 
investigate when an element of the hypercohomology space of a certain 
construction belongs to a symplectic sheaf. This is represented by a 
perfect complex of vector spaces. The theory is validated through 
applications to symplectic bundles, specifically resolving an open 
question regarding the symplectic nature of bundles of minimal rank 2 
over a K3 surface.

We employ generating functions to describe the set of all partitions with specific rules governing the multiplicity of each part, and use these functions to establish relationships between different partition categories. Furthermore, we leverage these connections to derive formulas for the Kostka matrix coefficients governing the decomposition of weighted partitions into partitioned partitions, specifically in scenarios where the original partition's parts have distinct sizes or multiplicities limited to two.

We examine a weighted least squares approach to high-dimensional linear regression and nonlinear function estimation, which becomes increasingly complex as its dimensions grow. Given the absence of categorization on the data samples, a new method assigns weights based on unknown quantity expectations, leading to a robust estimator that is stable and optimal within this framework. Under the assumption of smoothness in the regression, this estimator is shown to be consistent and asymptotically optimal when dimensions become infinitely large. The method assigns greater importance to uncertain data samples, effectively reducing the influence of outliers. A model-agnostic, cross-validation technique is developed to estimate the relevant parameters in practice, and the proposed estimator's performance is compared with existing methods through simulation studies.

Our previous calculation on X(3872) production in heavy-ion collisions is extended to address various aspects of X(3872) production. Specifically, we examined how the internal structure of X(3872) influences reaction rates and initial conditions within the hadronic phase, and considered D0 decay width implications, using a rate equation to determine yields and examining D/s ratios with varying X(3872) formation times and decay parameters. Additionally, the impact of X(3872) binding energy on D/s ratios was investigated, and the results were compared with theoretical models to understand the hadronic production of X(3872).

A comprehensive review of the properties and behaviors of defect moments in
semiconductors, specifically those in group IV materials, is presented. The role
of valence electrons interacting with cores via Kondo coupling is emphasized, as
well as the contrasting cases of magnetic and non-magnetic alloys. Research
on Si:dopants has yielded significant insights, particularly regarding the way
doping creates a self-consistent magnetic moment on heavily doped Si:P. By
examining the properties of group IV ferromagnets and studying quantum critical
behavior in Ge:Sn, this work delves into the broader implications of moment
behaviors in these semiconductors, ultimately seeking to understand the
general principles governing magnetic properties in this domain.

We derive exponential and logarithmic formulas for the generalized standard OGS of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, using a combinatorial approach based on its Coxeter length and descent set. These formulas express how the exchange law changes under a group homomorphism, or equivalently, how it is affected by a bihomomorphism when considering the twisted version. This involves a detailed analysis of the interplay between Coxeter length and descent set when applying the group homomorphism or a bihomomorphism, or when moving from Bn to Bn+1, or Bn to Gn, where Gn is the generalized Weyl group of type Bn, Cn, or Dn. These formulas have applications in a range of contexts, including the study of random exchanges within the group Bn and its generalizations, as well as Eulerian partitions of sets.

We determined the U(1) anomalous dimension and U(1) "diffusion constant" for scalar field theories in any dimension greater than or equal to 0, up to two loops in an arbitrary gauge. Our findings reveal that the U(1) current conserves the scalar field up to two loops in an explicit symmetry breaking context, similar to the massless Yukawa theory case. Furthermore, we found that the U(1) current conserves the complex scalar field in two-loop calculations for theories involving two complex scalars coupled with each other. Our results also reveal that the conservation of the U(1) current in massless two complex scalar theories is validated at the two-loop level in an arbitrary gauge.

When robots acquire skills through learning, real-world data often includes problems like noisy labels and hidden confounders that could mislead the process. A new hierarchical Bayesian approach resolves these issues by assuming the skill demonstration skill and the task-independent object characteristics share a common, latent skill. This latent skill helps in eliminating the confounders and simplifying the object model. System tests using simulated objects in diverse environments demonstrate that the new method yields better results compared to existing techniques.

Let $X$ be a topological space and $H$ be a collection of continuous functions from $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$, whose pointwise topology includes the set $H$. We define $\widetilde{X}_H$ as the set of functions $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ that can be expressed as a pointwise limit of functions in $H$. We also consider two topologies on $\widetilde{X}_H$: the whisker topology and the lasso topology, and investigate under which conditions these two topologies coincide. It is proven that this occurs when either the space $X$ is compact or the set $H$ meets a specific criterion. Conversely, a counterexample is given to show that these two topologies may not be equivalent even when the space $X$ is compact.

Recent research has shown that deep reinforcement learning can create skilled motion plans without pre-defined models, yet still relies on a pre-programmed set of possible actions. In our work, we eliminate the need for pre-set actions by incorporating a different stage in the learning process, using a model that can generate new movements on the fly. By doing so, we open the door for more efficient and effective motion planning, and demonstrate improved performance in challenging simulations of navigating a robot in a 2D environment.

The Eddington-limited mass flow into a black hole through a surrounding gas disk would significantly increase its mass over the course of a typical star-forming period, adding up to roughly one-tenth the mass of the gas in the disk. If a large portion of the gas in the center of a galaxy flows into a black hole over a star-forming period, this would imply a much stronger connection between a black hole's mass and a galaxy's total mass, which has been observed in the $M_{\rm black} - M_{\rm galaxy}$ relation. However, a large portion of the gas in a galaxy typically doesn't flow into a black hole; rather, most of it participates in star formation. As a result, another mechanism must be responsible for a galaxy's $M_{\rm black} - M_{\rm galaxy}$ relation. We propose that feedback from supermassive black holes could be responsible, as their energy output would prevent gas from settling into a disk around the black hole, redirecting it into the surrounding environment where it can participate in star formation. This would also remove any Eddington-limited influence on the black hole's mass growth.

Deep neural networks have gained popularity in recent years due to their ability to perform well on a variety of tasks, such as classification and data association. While successful, they often lack insight into their predictions. This poses a problem, particularly in situations requiring high stakes decision-making, where understanding the basis for a prediction is crucial. This paper explores the use of uncertainty quantification in class association tasks, specifically the MODD (Making From Data Distribution) task. We evaluated several uncertainty quantification methods, including Bayesian Neural Networks and adversarial training, on a modified version of the MNIST dataset. Our results indicate that combining a BNN with a robust post-processing step yields the best performance, and that adversarial training can be effective even without the need for robust post-processing. Furthermore, we found that using a BNN tends to produce softer outputs and fewer incorrect classifications when faced with adversarial attacks compared to a standard deep learning model.

The broad adoption of preprints is shifting the scientific sector's tradition, and it's crucial to measure the impact of preprints. This study conducted a substantial review of 34 studies that compared preprints to published articles across various fields, and our analysis indicates that preprints significantly boost the speed and citation levels of published research. Notably, authors whose work is posted online first or as a preprint experience further gains in citation counts. This study reveals that, generally, the advantages of preprints apply to both established and up-and-coming researchers, although some variables and fields show different outcomes. As a result, our findings suggest that disseminating research via preprints can be considered a established best practice in science. To facilitate decision-making, we provide decision support tools, like a decision tree, and guidelines to aid researchers, publishers, and policymakers navigating the preprint landscape, along with recommendations for policy changes that could further increase the preprint's potential.

One of the labor-intensive aspects of laboratory work is documenting results, which consumes roughly 50-70% of laboratory staff time. Despite the advancements in technology over the past 20 years, this process is still largely performed manually. We maintain that a significant portion of this documentation can be safely automated. To support this claim, we introduce a system designed to handle results documentation semi-automatically, using an advanced template-based approach. Our experience with this system, which has been in use at the Charité laboratory for over a year, is showcased through statistics and qualitative feedback from its users. We also outline potential avenues for further development, which could enhance the semi-automated process and its adoption in other laboratories.

The advent of machine learning has revolutionized the prediction of material properties, transforming the field of materials science and engineering. Through the analysis of publicly accessible databases and simulations, researchers can now utilize data-driven methods to forecast materials' composition, crystal and magnetic phase formations, and a wide range of mechanical, electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties. This review showcases the success of machine learning in addressing complex materials issues, highlighting its applications in simulating phase transformations, modeling materials properties, discovering new materials, and understanding materials dynamics. Furthermore, the review discusses the existing challenges and future prospects for machine learning in materials science, identifying areas such as uncertainty quantification, time series prediction, and dynamic scenario modeling as promising directions for research.
