These findings support the use of EuS/InAs interface in spintronics and magneto-optics, producing a magnetically induced optical transition at the InAs bandedge.

We establish a specific instance of a significant hypothesis in set theory, known as the Godel-Lorenzen hypothesis, as equivalent to a more refined notion of truth, and therefore to other more general ideas of truth that have been discussed in the existing body of research. This refined notion of truth is stricter than those previously proposed and is not comparable to some other, more relaxed concepts of truth that have been explored. Notably, Borel Wadge determinacy, a concept more general than the refined notion of truth, has far-reaching consequences, including the ability to prove the consistency of second-order arithmetic and the existence of large cardinal axioms such as the existence of stationary sets that are not reflectable. Furthermore, the existence of a refined notion of truth implies the existence of an even larger type of stationary set, a result that contrasts with previous research findings on the themes of middle killing and stationary reflective posets.

Recent advances in model pruning have yielded impressive results, with typical methods achieving notable training gains while leading to reduced inference performance. However, this limitation hinders the use of these techniques in real-world applications. Our research introduces ClickTrain, a novel training algorithm based on node sparsity, designed to boost both training and inference efficiency. Unlike previous approaches, ClickTrain adapts its training strategy according to the current pruning phase, ensuring optimal results. Additionally, we developed ClickTrain's counterpart for model inference, which outperforms traditional methods, with our experiments demonstrating significant gains in both training and inference speed. Notably, ClickTrain's effects are orthogonal to other pruning techniques, enabling the use of previously pruned models without requiring re-training.

We develop a relational semantics for substructural modal logics by adapting Kripke models to incorporate both modal and substructural features. Our proposed semantics is decoded into corresponding axioms and, as a result, provides proof strategies for verifying key properties of these logics. The proposed relational semantics can be configured to reflect both the weak and the fuzzy versions of the logic.

The merger of a neutron star pair, whether from a coalescing binary or a large mass neutron star, leads to the generation of a broad spectrum of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation. This rare astronomical event may have been responsible for the observed fast-rise luminosity, lasting about a week, in the AT2017gfo system. To better comprehend neutron star mergers, models need to efficiently transport energy at incredible rates, exceeding $10^{52}$ erg s$^{-1}$. Our novel model proposes a viscous boundary layer near the boundary of the boundary layer and the accretion disk that can efficiently transfer energy on a small scale, supported by our 3D simulations, which demonstrate efficient energy propagation through the boundary layer. This model also explains how magnetic stress, weakened by viscosity, is transferred and ultimately facilitates energy transfer. Furthermore, we observe the growth of vortices in our simulations, which could significantly impact various physical processes.

TOI-5542b holds significant potential for compositional and conceptual research in planetary science due to its large size and proximity to Sun-like stars. A valuable resource for scientists is the TESS mission, which offers the possibility of identifying a planetary object similar to that of Jupiter's in size, orbiting a star that is similar to the Sun, and is located close to our planet. Not long after the initial detection, follow-up studies were conducted using the APOGEE-2 and MOA survey, and further confirmed by other observations. They revealed a remarkable match in their data, which suggested the presence of a gas giant planet. This fact led to the creation of a transit fit model, and a new analysis that combined radiative and energetic inputs, which provided significant insights. This research was further discussed based on various constraints, and it is expected that future missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope will provide a more in-depth understanding of the planet's properties.

Our new algorithm generates actionable policies for complex stochastic decision problems by utilizing a primal-dual approach and sampling. It takes the form of an online learning algorithm, specifically a bandit algorithm, which can be implemented in a sequential manner. By leveraging the strength of our algorithm in handling general decision problems, we show its effectiveness in tackling minimax stochastic learning problems, including those involving Robuc and Minimax-SL. Experimental results reveal that our algorithm successfully produces operational policies that outperform alternative methods, particularly in generating off-policy actions for robotic planning.

We've prepared a dataset of 3011 mathematical symbol images, along with their LaTeX code, to facilitate research in mathematical symbol recognition. Unlike conventional datasets, our stars are the intricate and diverse range of mathematical symbols, often found in scientific publications. We've selected a k-Nearest Neighbor classifier as the benchmark model to test the effectiveness of various feature extraction techniques. We hope this dataset contributes to the advancement of mathematical symbol recognition, a vital area with potential applications in scientific literature automation. The dataset is available for public use at https://github.com/JoaoBBethel/Mathematica/tree/main/MATHS7600.

We investigate the pattern of physical state selection within the theory, focusing on BPS state variables. This is achieved through the correlation of two key concepts: the phase of the central charge $\phi$ and the sign of the Hessian. For the D1-D3-D5 system, an analytical framework is developed to determine how the number and degeneracy of BPS states shift as a function of $\phi$ and Hessian signs, without requiring a particle basis. This non-linear relationship is treated using the Hilbert scheme of $C^2$, parameterized by $K$ points, and through this parameterization, we're able to explain the rapid growth of BPS state degeneracies via index, as well as the concentration of these states around specific charge phases. This analytical approach extends beyond the standard $\mathcal{N}=4$ and semi-self-dual cases. Furthermore, we've made available an independent verification tool, written in Mathematica, to manually calculate and binate the isospectral BPS states for any given set of charge parameters.

Understanding and measuring network connectivity is vital for predicting and controlling the spread of epidemics. We have developed a method to quantify a network's connectivity by analyzing the spread of a non-contact disease, which can be applied to real-world scenarios. According to our results, a network's structure that facilitates multiple connected components is ideal for predicting the spread of a epidemic, as it presents opportunities for targeted interventions. Conversely, a network with a compact structure that facilitates swift disease transmission is more challenging to predict. Furthermore, our method can be coupled with the core principle of contact tracing to estimate the dissemination of a disease. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we have conducted extensive simulations on various network configurations, including scale-free and random networks, and obtained results that align with the fundamental principles of epidemicology.

We introduce SafetyQ, an open-source library for endpoint detection in reinforcement learning (RL) that integrates with existing solutions such as DeepRO and DeepSafe. SafetyQ ends an agent's episode when it encounters a critical safety breach, which is triggered by either a safety violation detected by the agent or a predetermined deadline. This framework is designed to address a common challenge in RL known as the "return gap" problem, where the reward signals may not adequately motivate safe behavior. To bridge this gap, SafetyQ accelerates the learning process by safely terminating suboptimal episodes, which is particularly beneficial for deep RL experiments where episode lengths can be substantial. This framework is highly adaptable and compatible with a range of return signals, including negative infinite returns. Additionally, SafetyQ is versatile in its implementation and can be used in both on-policy and off-policy settings, making it a universally applicable tool. Furthermore, SafetyQ's safety detection mechanism can be extended to include additional features such as safety violations triggered by post-episode assessments. This extension enables the safe reuse of pre-trained models.

We develop a novel approach using random number generation to identify twin primes by introducing a Twin Prime Theorem. This method is based on a general concept known as the Twin Prime Conjecture. Our method focuses on a specific aspect of twin primes by considering the primary factors that contribute to their occurrence. This focus allows us to identify a key element - the common factor of twin primes' differences - which in turn leads to the development of a probabilistic tool. This tool, based on relative primes and modular arithmetic, helps us derive precise probability bounds for twin primes within a specified range. However, as the range increases, the probability fluctuates between two bounds as predicted by the Central Limit Theorem and Geometric Distribution properties. Ultimately, we define a Twin Prime Theorem which states that as the prime number's upper limit approaches infinity, the probability of twin primes within that range converges to a specific non-zero value. This result is validated using analytical methods and supporting graphs. Furthermore, we refine the Twin Prime Theorem by considering Lagrange's Four Square Theorem, developing a more precise probabilistic bound in the process. This revised bound is the primary outcome of our work.

We have developed a layered control system that separates navigation and control into distinct components, using sonar sensors to facilitate efficient collision avoidance on mobile platforms. By implementing control and navigation independently, we achieve improved stability and robustness, ultimately enabling successful execution of swarming maneuvers within a simulated environment.

Nereid, the largest moon of Neptune, has been observed by the JWST, providing the first direct look at its behavior since 1989. During these encounters, Nereid's appearance was unexpected, offering clues about its irregular orbit. Recent images taken by JWST on May 12, 2023, reveal Nereid's bright blue color, offering insights into its properties and the possible presence of methane or tholins on its surface. This is the first visual evidence of Nereid's properties since 1989, and the findings present a unique opportunity for future observations, potentially paving the way for a future lunar mission.

We examine a representable permutation group acting on the projective line over a ring, and investigate conditions under which it can be extended to a projective plane. Furthermore, we discuss how affine planes constructed from the projective line over a ring can be extended to projective planes.

We introduce a novel approach to the Tukey-order for ideas within Ramsey theory, expand upon the concept of model Tukey-order and establish methods to prove the interdependence of various cardinal properties in set theory. This method has significant potential for uncovering the intricate relationships between different properties and can be used to solve prominent open problems in the field. Some of these applications have already been identified, while others are proposed as conjectures.

We've developed a novel extension to Thompson sampling that combines its probabilistic approach with a pessimistic outlook, enabling an algorithm that can efficiently learn the optimal dynamic treatment policy even in complex situations. By incorporating a pessimistic element, our method creates a local minimax estimate of the treatment policy, but similar to Thompson sampling, its confidence bounds remain asymptotically relevant. We've established the first and second-order statistical guarantees for our algorithm, and through experiments in tough scenarios, it outperforms standard Thompson sampling, often significantly so. We've even derived a practical variant that's efficient enough for large-scale applications, and shown its guarantees to be asymptotically identical to those of the exact method. Finally, in simulated environments, our algorithm surpasses alternatives, and its approximating variant closely mirrors its performance.

We establish the invariance of higher algebraic K-groups under changes to a resolving subcategory of finitely generated modules. This invariance holds when the changing subcategory is replaced by a subcategory of finitely presented modules with no free modules. Our proof relies on a novel reformation of the Bass exact sequence, similar to its analogue for triangulated categories. This reformulated Bass exact sequence is applied to modules and gives rise to an equivariant version. This equivariant version can be used to reprove the invariance of algebraic K-groups under category changes for modules with no free modules. This reproof offers clearer insights into the category of modules than the existing proof based on Quillen's equivalence.

We establish a formal framework that allows for a controlled transformation of one quantum state configuration into another, leveraging contextuality in high-dimensional systems. This framework enables us to identify and manipulate nonlocal connections among different state configurations in quantum mechanics, effectively allowing for a "quantum erase" operation to eradicate nonlocality and contextuality within a desired state configuration. Furthermore, our framework enables the exploration of nonlocality and contextuality in experiments involving sequential state measurements.

Using exact diagonalization, we investigate the properties of Hubbard models with multi-band configurations, focusing on etapairing states. This etapairing exhibits a particle-hole symmetry characteristic, similar to d-wave pairing, and we reveal how "strong" etapairing correlates with particle-hole coupling through interband interactions at half and quarter filling. Furthermore, etapairing persists beyond small clusters in certain cases and we examine the impact of decoherence on etapairing in larger clusters.

We solve a functional equation that is analogous to the generalized Polya theorem in the context of Q-algebra theory, specifically for adic solenoids. The solution involves a type of function that is similar to those in the theorem, and we are able to express it using series of Dirac delta functions. The proof relies on a method of consecutive approximations, and we are able to establish that any function which can be expressed in the form of an adic polynomial divided by a regular positive adic-holomorphic function can satisfy the given functional equation.

Analysis of species occurrence data is increasingly being used in ecological studies, yet widely varied methods complicate comparison and assessment of results. To address this, we evaluated the performance of eight clustering techniques applied to same-data sets across multiple studies, testing four solutions with respect to mask creation and cluster identification. Our investigation considered the influence of different mask approaches – binary, fuzzy, and presence-absence with error margins – and cluster resolution strategies, including maximum similarity and merged clusters. The evaluation criteria encompassed six key factors: effectiveness, stability, ease of use, required expertise, computational demands, and output interpretability. Our aims were to provide insights into how these methods compare and suggest future research directions, with the ultimate goal of promoting informed data analysis and interpretation.

Process and optimize RGB and RGB-D images efficiently to detect salient objects. A unified structure is proposed that simultaneously processes RGB and RGB-D images within a single network, thereby allowing for rapid and precise object extraction from both RGB and RGB-D data. The proposed structure is called the Unified Deep Suppression Network, or UDS-Net for short. It combines RGB and depth features through explicit fusion, which enables the identification of key features common to both types of data. The integration of salient object detection with depth features is shown to significantly improve the precision of this process, based on analysis of multiple datasets. Furthermore, the structure is capable of generating high-quality output across a wide range of scales, without the need for post-processing. The benefits of this approach are measured in terms of efficiency, as measured by network size, and in terms of precision, as measured by metrics such as intersection over union. Evaluations indicate a trade-off between these factors, known as the balance between efficiency and performance, which is a key characteristic of this method. Evaluations are performed on several large-scale datasets, which are publicly available, and the results show that the UDS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics and datasets.

We've explored the NLP tasks of sentiment analysis and information extraction in response to an inquiry from Google about addressing online abuse. As part of our exploration, we addressed two key challenges: identifying abusive content and categorizing the forms of online toxicity. Our focus was on supervised approaches, with data consisting of annotated tweets obtained from Wikipedia articles. Our primary goal was to determine whether these articles could be utilized effectively in detecting abusive content. To this end, we employed various text representation methods and optimized models, before presenting our findings in the form of a technical report rather than submitting a paper to the NLP4ME workshop. Despite initial reservations about the efficacy of our approaches, our best efforts achieved a macro F1 score of 0.754 for detecting abusive content and 0.734 for categorizing online toxicity.

Consider a number sequence where each element has the form $10a+b$ and both $a$ and $b$ range from 0 to 9. Numbers of this form that are palindromic in the decimal system are referred to as 10-palindromes or simply palindromes for brevity. Numbers that cannot be expressed as 10-palindromes in the decimal system are referred to as unrepresentable integers. We calculate the density of unrepresentable integers within this number sequence and determine the density to be approximately 0.1378.

Reconstructing high-quality images from noisy, limited-angle data in computed tomography (CT) poses a difficult problem, largely because standard personalizable image reconstruction methods are vulnerable to noise and may produce artificially low-density areas. To address this challenge, this research introduces the limited-angle, personalizable, and noisy (LAPN) network, a new data-driven model specifically designed to tackle limited-angle, noisy data. PAI methods typically rely on statistical noise models that are simplistic and inadequate, but the proposed LAPN model leverages a neural network to accurately characterize personal and shared features in image data. To personalize images under the constraint of limited-angle data, LAPN uses an unrolling framework that incorporates personalized and common updates. Furthermore, LAPN's unrolling framework can be trained end-to-end with a backpropagation algorithm, and end-to-end training allows the network to accurately characterize personal and shared features, as well as to personalize images from limited-angle data. We tested the proposed LAPN model on simulated data and compared its performance to that of the iterative simultaneous algebraic-ordering-of-matrices (iSARAM) method, a state-of-the-art method that uses 20 iterations. The results show that LAPN outperforms iSARAM at various signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), and we also developed two extensions to further improve the model's performance.

Automated handwriting is a complex task that programs are struggling to complete, largely due to a lack of adequate data. The Bayesian Program Learning framework holds promise in addressing this challenge by generating program inputs that adhere to Bayesian Program Guidelines, resulting in more efficient search and learning processes. A new study builds upon BPL's capabilities by incorporating a prior distribution on program inputs known as Bayesian Program with a Cost. This advanced method involves maximizing the program's likelihood by minimizing unnecessary steps, facilitating better exploration of the program search space. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of BPL in writing minimal, scale-invariant handwriting after just one training iteration. Moreover, BPWC outperforms conventional Bayesian Program learning by producing more accurate outputs on three distinct handwriting datasets. BPWC also enhances program robustness by preventing data contamination from unexpected inputs, showcasing its potential in secure program design. Finally, BPWC is applied to an challenging real-world task: generating automatic signatures, highlighting its practical value in real-world settings.

A newly devised storage scheme efficiently stores the computed three-nucleon interaction coefficients, thereby enabling rapid retrieval and calculation of their values during numerical computations. Derived from a mathematical representation of the interaction's orbital part, this storage method significantly reduces the memory required to store the coefficients. In contrast to the traditional band diagonal form's storage demand, which scales with the square of the nuclear model space size, this novel approach only scales linearly. For example, in a model space of approximately 6000 dimensions, this scheme reduces memory requirements by over five orders of magnitude. Notably, most of this reduction in memory demand comes from eliminating the storage of nearly zero values. This improvement enables the computation of more intricate three-nucleon interactions within reach. A computational example is provided, where we calculated all possible 16-body operators involving the effective two-body interaction, the Coulomb force, and spin-orbit forces within the 2p2s model space.

In the past decade, research in quantum electronics has accelerated, and several advanced concepts such as nanomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and quantum point contacts have been incorporated into nano-electronic technology. The understanding of quantum electronics is enhanced by the method of correlators and von-Neumann density-matrix method, which both utilize the Green's function formalism to describe non-equilibrium quantum systems. These methods not only provide clear physical explanations for the equilibrium and non-equilibrium properties of quantum electronics but also offer effective tools for analyzing quantum transport and generating quantum entanglement. The applicability of these methods has been applied to the analysis of nanomechanical resonators, and we demonstrate that entanglement can be generated between the vibration and electric charge.

Let D be a bounded convex domain in n-dimensional complex space, with its real boundary denoted as ∂D. This study focuses on non-degenerate bounded linear operators T, T-1, and C, the composition operator with symbol f, within the space of analytic functions analytic on D (also denoted as H(A(D))) and its closed subspace consisting of functions that have a specific rate of growth (denoted as A∞(D)). It is proven that T, T-1, and C are all dense in the space of bounded linear operators from A(Δ) to A(Δ), with Δ a 2-dimensional bounded convex domain, given the presence of non-trivial analytic discs in ∂D.

In string theory, the GEPSC model's two-loop corrections to twist-four operators' anomalous dimensions are calculated, specifically for spin-two and spin-zero operators. This involves computing the transcendental weights of world-sheet one-loop amplitudes, which are solved using the Birkhoff decomposition technique to derive finite-world-sheet mechanisms. This research explores an extension of the duality between string theory and a conformal field theory, relating GEPSC mode functions to a conformal framework. The findings also address potential kinematic mass deformations in twist-four operators' evolution.

Most deep learning frameworks rely on dynamic memory allocation on the GPU to efficiently handle variable-sized data structures, such as neuron tensors in a neural network's forward pass. However, the standard GPU memory allocators provided by CUDA and other frameworks lead to excessive, unnecessary memory allocations and cause memory leaks. A new, more efficient dynamic memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed, offering substantial performance improvements and superior memory usage to traditional allocators. By adapting a segment-based approach from Sun Microsystems' malloc library to the GPU, DynaSOAr enhances memory allocation efficiency while minimizing both the number of memory blocks and the overhead from heap management operations. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's parallelization structure enables seamless integration with modern GPU architectures, outperforming traditional allocators by up to 2.5 times and reducing the number of memory allocations by up to 3 orders of magnitude in tests.

Dark matter that doesn't follow the rules of charge (isospin violation in dark matter) can occur in certain models that use an additional electrical charge (U(1)_X), especially when the charge's strength isn't too high or too low. Isospin breaking in dark matter interactions can happen directly or indirectly, for example, through differences in mass between types of dark particles. However, this theory of multiple dark particles with varying masses is limited by constraints from experiments that look at nuclear interactions, specifically by requiring that the dark particles don't create too many particles when they interact with nuclei. On the other hand, indirect detection experiments such as Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer may have observed a signal consistent with both dark particles interacting with matter in a specific way, including differences in how they interact with various targets. An alternative to the standard two-dark-particle model, especially in U(1)_X, involves creating dark particles in pairs, including a particle that decays into other particles and another that doesn't, which can explain a signal seen by Fermi Satellite without conflicting with experiments that look at nuclear interactions, specifically by requiring that the two dark particles have significantly different masses and interactions with matter. Both of these approaches to isospin violation in dark matter provide new ways to understand a signal seen by Fermi Satellite and the remaining part of the 270 GeV dark matter signal seen by AMS.

The behavior of straw tubes in a vacuum environment is influenced by their elastic properties and the force exerted by the electric field on charged particles. Research into simplified models of straw geometry has shown that the minimum pre-tension required to prevent tube collapse is directly proportional to the tube's eccentricity under pre-stressed conditions. However, this and other simplified models' predictions fall short in accounting for the tube's shape and the force it undergoes in a curved state. Moreover, these models are insufficient in understanding the dynamics of particle trajectories and particle confinement in a straw tube. This study aims to provide a precise mathematical and numerical analysis of straw geometry and particle behavior, focusing on the role of pre-tension and electric field on particle confinement.

We propose a formal framework to evaluate the reliability of decision-making functions in situations involving uncertainty about the underlying parameters. Our framework enables the calculation of a lower bound on the likelihood that a decision-making function will remain effective, even when subjected to varying levels of parameter uncertainty. We apply this framework to study the robustness of decision functions in statistics and machine learning, including the impact of parameter uncertainty on the support of a distribution. Our results are demonstrated through analyses of classical statistical problems and learning algorithms, such as Bayesian decision-making and the k-nearest neighbors method.

The oscillatory movement of an impurity within a supersolid is studied theoretically by employing impurity scattering techniques. Two distinct models of impurity behavior are examined: one which experiences strong coupling to phonon modes and another with coupling limited by a cutoff frequency. For the first model, the presence of an impurity significantly impacts phonon behavior, altering the shape of the roton minimum and changing the phonon dispersion near the roton. However, the second model reveals a more modest influence. Further analysis indicates that the supersolid's dissipation of energy due to impurity scattering is diminished by the rapid oscillations of the impurity. Finally, the role of impurity crystallographic site in the supersolid's degradation is also considered.

A neighbour-transitive code in a geometric design or generalised quadrangle implies adjacent-code transitivity as well. Focusing on neighbour-transitive codes within generalized quadrangles of order $q$, a comprehensive code collection is presented for $q = 2^m$ or $q = 3^m$. Additionally, existing class tables for the Weyl group of type $D_4$ and Weyl group of type $G_2$ are used to determine neighbour-transitive codes of order $q = 4^m$ and $q = 3^m$ respectively.

We investigated the density variation within one degree of the Central Molecular Zone's eastern portion, using a extensive molecular data set, by calculating angular distances and logarithmic densities across various scales ranging from 0.3 to 10 degrees.  These calculations resulted in density maps across different scales, where we found that certain structures appear flattened at larger scales but become more compact at smaller scales.  The Anisotropy Structure Function showed that density distribution becomes more uniform as scales increase, where significant density variations persist up to 10 degrees.  The Non-Local Source Term of the Minkowski Process also indicated that there are significant anisotropies at larger scales.  Furthermore, by examining the contributions of individual molecular complexes, we found that those with stronger radio continuum emission have stronger logarithmic density gradients.  We then applied a fractal analysis to the density maps and found that the Central Molecular Zone exhibits scale-invariant properties across all scales.  However, the density distribution is more pronounced at smaller scales and less pronounced at larger scales.  Based on these findings, we suggest that the Central Molecular Zone may be the result of multiple gas accretions onto a primordial stellar cluster formed about 10 million years ago.

The interaction between intense laser radiation and metal targets is a complex phenomenon that affects both the target and its surrounding electron cloud. Our study examines how electrons are affected when a high-intensity laser beam interacts with a metallic nickel target. Using a full-range relativistic particle simulations, we simulate various laser intensities and energies, and find that changes in the metal's absorption coefficient at high energies are significantly influenced by the redistribution of electrons. Additionally, we discover that a sudden increase in the metal's absorption coefficient occurs when the laser-induced electron cloud reaches a critical threshold, and this process is comparable to the generation of coherent X-rays through plasma processes. However, this absorption change is brief, as the metal's plasma wave is quickly damped out. In contrast, lower-energy electrons that remain in the metal's absorption coefficient exhibit a slower decrease, and this co-exists with a significant increase in the metal's absorption coefficient at higher energies. This dual behavior is influenced by the electron's momentum and charge, and provides a potential explanation for observed discrepancies in the experiment's results on nickel targets.

A tiny temperature sensor built with only 124 transistors accurately measures temperature across a broad range (0 to 120°C) with minimal error, particularly when temperatures are high (below 1°C). The sensor's efficiency was maximized by implementing a new temperature-to-voltage conversion method that eliminates the need for an analog-to-digital converter. The sensor features a straightforward interface and operates at a low current consumption of 4.2 μA. The sensor's performance was validated using a single chip, 0.18 μm CMOS process with an adequate level of precision. Although the sensor's resolution and inaccuracy aren't on par with typical sensor specifications, its efficiency makes it a viable option for applications requiring accurate thermal monitoring in small devices.

A combination of single-photon sources, beam splitters, and quantum measurements enables the preparation of entangled states within the context of quantum information. By employing linear optics and post-selection, it remains possible to create complex multi-party correlations despite the lack of control over coherent states. We demonstrate an experimental technique called "quantum scissors" that refines this process to produce highly correlated states of polarized photons in a system of three and four particles. This advancement represents a significant improvement in the efficiency of entanglement generation and extends the scope of available entangled states, thus facilitating research into the properties of complex entangled systems.

For distributing shortest paths in undirected graphs, the problem of exact shortest paths, it has been long established through linear programming that the competitive ratio cannot be lower than $\Omega(\log n / \log \log n)$ in online algorithms, where $n$ is the number of vertices. Despite extensive efforts, the optimal online algorithm in various dimensions remains unsolved.

In our study, we explore the possibility of allowing the online algorithm to select Steiner points in addition to vertices, in order to distribute shortest paths. Our research provides the first evidence that the lower bound of the competitive ratio can be higher than the initial bound, $\Omega(\log n / \log \log n)$ in dimension two, and $\Omega(\log \log n / \log n)$ in dimensions three and above. In dimension two, the new algorithm has a competitive ratio of $\frac{\log n}{\log \log n} - 2$, in dimension three, the ratio is $\frac{\log \log n}{\log n} + \frac{1}{2}\log \log n - 1$, in dimension four, the ratio is $\frac{\log \log n}{\log n} - 1 - \frac{\log 2}{\log \log n} - 1$, in dimension five, the ratio is $\frac{\log \log n}{\log n} - 2 - \frac{\log 2}{\log \log n} -

As IoT devices continue to grow at a rapid pace, managing and securing these devices becomes increasingly crucial. While existing research on IoT device classification has made significant progress, it has also raised more complex questions. One of the key challenges is to develop an cost-effective approach to classify IoT devices with varying costs attached to accurate and incorrect classifications. However, this leads to another important concern, which is to prevent excessive misclassification that might result in disproportionate financial losses. To address these complexities, we propose a new method called the Cost-Risk Ratio (CRR), which not only takes into consideration the cost of classification but also limits the impact of costly misclassifications. By implementing the CRR, we have created an adversarial attack strategy that forces IoT devices into specific false categories while minimizing misclassification costs. Through our experiments using ABED and EMBER datasets, we have found that our CRR-based method achieves higher success rates in forced misclassification and limits costs compared to existing approaches.

This study provides a comprehensive description of the algebraic and logical characteristics of finite G\"odel algebras, revealing that these algebras are equivalent to the concept of finite forests. Furthermore, it is proven that the standard Stone dualities for finite G\"odel and Heyting algebras can be jointly generalized into a single dual theory, known as the Boolean-Algebraic-Dual theory. As a direct consequence, the existing dualities for finite G\"odel and Heyting algebras can be derived from this unified framework.

We develop a parametric aligner named Garbaggio that employs a novel
approximation method for the alignement of two sequences as well as a range
of simplifications to reduce the complexity of the alignment problem, which
is known to be NP-complete. Garbaggio's performance is evaluated on a dataset
of 16 languages from Wikipedia, but due to computational constraints, the
alignment is only optimal for languages with a small corpus, namely English
and French. Our results indicate that Garbazzo produces high-quality alignments
comparable to established tools, such as GIZA++ and gnugettext. Notably,
our approach offers a significant speed improvement over these algorithms,
notably a 3.5 times speedup over GIZA++ and an 8 times speedup over gnugettext.
In addition, Garbazzo's alignments correlate strongly with human-generated
annotations, suggesting that its results are of sufficient accuracy to support
machine translation tasks.

The asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm is an alternative method for solving block-structured nonlinear problems. It utilizes the principles of B-analysis from nonstandard analysis and works by implementing a modified Asmussen-Da Prato type lifting technique. Our study focuses on deriving meaningful bounds for the speed of convergence of the asynchronous algorithm. We also examine its applicability to specific problem types, such as monotone inclusion and split variational inequality, and provide examples of its implementation.

Our research explores the possibility that stellar-mass black hole lensing events detected by the upcoming Lucy and WFIRST missions could be a result of primordial black holes rather than regular black holes. We've calculated the predicted number of PBH and stellar-mass black hole lensing events based on current observations of stellar-mass black hole mergers and the characteristics of PBHs. Assuming a PBH mass of 30 solar masses, we estimate that Lucy and WFIRST will detect 30 times more PBH lensing events than stellar-mass black hole lensing events. We've also determined the parameters of the PBH mass function that would provide sufficient evidence for PBH existence, and considered the impact of uncertainties in the model. We've found that LISA and the planned high-cadence space-based telescope for mid-frequency gravitational waves, named Via Lactoria, could provide further evidence for PBH existence by detecting around 11 LISA events and 1-4 mid-frequency signals per decade. We've concluded that LISA and the upcoming Lucy and WFIRST missions have the potential to provide sufficient evidence for PBH existence, and that further data will help reduce the uncertainties in the model.

This research investigates the equilibrium shape and stacking sequence of hexagonal packing, specifically focusing on the thermodynamic properties of polar crystalline phases as a function of particle packing density. Through extensive simulations, we revealed a rich phase diagram that includes various polar and frustrated polar phases. Our main findings are the existence of two distinct frustrated polar phases - type I and type II - which appear at a packing density above 0.5 and are characterized by unique collective movements. Notably, these phases exhibit helical structures that reverse at a finite temperature, accompanied by distinct enthalpy and entropy changes. In contrast, the type I phase features a single, unified pattern with helices of equal size, whereas the type II phase comprises alternating packs of long and short helices. As the packing density increases, the temperature-dependent movement in the frustrated polar phase gradually diminishes until it coexists with a stable polar phase at a critical density of 0.54. Our results also show that this transition from a frustrated to a stable polar phase is accompanied by a sharp drop in the associated entropy and enthalpy changes.

This research investigates how various mathematical operations affect the positive definiteness of zonal functions. It is demonstrated that differentiating or integrating these functions retains positive definiteness, a beneficial property in statistics for constructing probability measures. Conversely, the convolution of two positive definite zonal functions is positive definite only if one of the functions is identically zero. Furthermore, the study reveals that positive definiteness is preserved under radial contraction and dilation, but not generally under transitive transformations. A key finding is that any positive definite function can be expressed as a Fourier series involving Bessel functions, enabling the construction of probability measures through polynomial approximations. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the Fourier kernel and Bessel kernel series representations.

Quantum imaging has the potential to greatly reduce the impact of light on sensitive specimens that can only interact with light in brief moments. Our approach to resolving this issue is based on an interaction-free imaging technique that uses a series of detections on a screen, along with probabilistic algorithms to reconstruct the sample or object. Since the sample only interacts with light momentarily, we consider its state as transient and utilize a new theoretical framework for dealing with non-stationary objects. This framework allows us to obtain unique images of both stationary and moving objects using only point-scanning or full-image detection methods. Our experiments confirm that this technique produces high-quality images of both static and dynamically changing objects.

We have developed a theoretical model for predicting the dynamic viscosity and pressure-drop across-fiber bedding force in liquid foams, formulated in terms of the roughness factor and surface tension. To verify our roughness factor definition, we conducted an experimental study using a specific foam solution, which showed that the roughness factor can be quantified as the product of the root mean square angle deviation and the fiber spacing. Furthermore, our numerical results for the dynamic viscosity and pressure-drop across-fiber bedding force align with previously reported experimental data and numerical simulations, indicating a strong correlation with the roughness factor.

Convolutional neural networks are highly effective at performing image classification, but their training can be challenging due to high computational costs and limited data availability. To overcome these difficulties, we propose an innovative approach that combines an ensemble of convolutional neural networks with a probabilistic voting system, fueled by chess-inspired insights. Our method draws inspiration from the winning strategies of famous chess players like AlphaZero and EMCTSL, adapting their concepts to the realm of deep learning. By incorporating diverse convolutional neural networks with distinct architectural variations and optimized parameters, our ensemble-based approach surpasses the performance of individual networks and legacy classification techniques, such as support vector machines and residual networks. Furthermore, the ensemble's decision-making process is facilitated by a weighted vote that prioritizes the influence of each network based on their individual accuracies, thus ensuring the most effective contributors take center stage. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, we conducted a comprehensive set of experiments across three image classification datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Fashion MNIST, showcasing impressive results that validate the strengths of our proposed method.

The excitation spectra of sodium dimers were investigated using a coupled-cluster approach for a range of interatomic distances. Our findings are consistent with experimental results from electron photoionization studies and show that dipolar electron-hole excitations are more heavily affected by static correlations than monopole hole excitations. Notably, the mass of these dipolar electron-hole excitations is significantly lower than that of monopole hole excitations and even approaches the mass of protons at shorter distances. This is attributed to the complex nature of dipolar excitations, which are influenced by long-range correlations throughout the dimer. The importance of accurately modeling these correlations is highlighted, and we demonstrate that perturbative correction methods can greatly improve the precision of our results, especially for shorter distances.

In this study, we establish a probabilistic framework for thermodynamic systems using a phase-space approach. We define a system's state as a probability distribution, $\rho$, in phase space, and a dynamical system, $\mathcal{S}(\rho, t)$, governed by a Hamiltonian, $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{q}, \mathrm{p})$, whose dynamics in phase space are driven by the Liouville equation. We show that the system's state, $\rho$, evolves over time, and define a work function, $\mathrm{W}(\rho, t)$, which is computed as the average of the Hamiltonian, $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{q}, \mathrm{p})$, with respect to $\rho$. We call this quantity the dissipated work and relate it to a system's internal microwork, which is computed as the average of the gradient of the Hamiltonian, $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{q}, \mathrm{p})$, with respect to $\rho$. We find that the dissipated work, $\mathrm{W}(\rho, t)$, is equal to the system's entropy production, $\sigma(\rho, t)$, and that the internal microwork, $\mu(\rho, t)$, is equal to the system's thermodynamic force, $\mathcal{F}(\rho, t)$. This brief note offers a straightforward calculation of cotangent bundle cotangent
spaces, specifically focusing on the cotangent space of matrices. It also computes
symplectic moment maps and curvature weights for the simple group U(1) and represents
these weights in a simple matrix form, analogous to the standard form used for Lie groups.
This calculation was inspired by a recent article of C. Toen and his collaborators (
arXiv:0211153).

Our study focuses on the long-wave behavior of inelastic diatomic Hertzian chains. We're particularly interested in the spectral analysis of these chains when they're quasi-localized near one specific site. This site acts as a "soft" point due to its larger spring constant, and we're examining the dynamics of two slightly oscillatory states born out of a small perturbation near this soft point. Under certain conditions, including a specific choice of displacement and velocity for the hard point, our quasi-localized states evolve into localized solitary waves, analogous to the well-studied Peierls regime in solid-state physics. This new regime shares similarities with the "swimming" mode observed in nonlinearly interacting phonons, where the hard point plays a crucial role in the phonon's phase and propagation direction. We've also shown that the wave patterns in this soft-potential well can be accurately represented using a Hamiltonian system defined by a pair of time-dependent equations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the weak-coupling Hamiltonian system in capturing the long-wave, quasi-localized behavior of the original inelastic chain.

Inflaton models featuring sudden changes, such as abrupt changes in velocity or potential, may occur either way. We've discovered that these abrupt changes, whether in a sudden velocity shift or potential change, result in identical effects on primordial non-Gaussian signatures using a specific local model. This equivalence has significant implications, as it may be easier to experimentally verify a specific inflation scenario, the Dirac-Born-Infeld model, which also features such sudden changes.

The Accordion Graph Class $A\left[ n; k \right]$ is defined by a set of standard accordions and a circular arrangement of k of them. We examine the circulant properties of this graph class. It is established that for $n \geq 4k+1$, the accordion graph is circulant. Conversely, it is shown that for $n < 4k+1$, the graph is not circulant. Moreover, the circulant properties of various standard accordion graphs are determined individually.

This study investigates the dynamics of a two-state quantum walk within a one-dimensional array of N sites, with periodic boundary conditions, using an anisotropic evolution operator. The walk is triggered by an initial superposition of the first two states, and we examine the long-term behavior as N approaches infinity. We focus on the average momentum and participation ratio as key performance metrics, and our analysis is based on a wave function with spatial symmetry. By averaging these metrics over all possible wave functions, we are able to determine the optimal detuning angles and corresponding steady-state values. We observe that the participation ratio remains low near the optimal detrapping angle and quickly increases as the angle deviates from this point. Beyond this discovery, the research also explores the dynamics of a similar model within a semi-infinite array of sites and reveals similar trends in the coherance loss.

This study examines the effectiveness of the DINO self-supervised method in improving ImageNet performance for pre-trained Vision Transformers. DINO has emerged as a straightforward yet highly effective approach to obtaining robust self-supervised representations from pre-trained Vision Transformers. Our research aims to explore DINO's limitations and assess its applicability to various pre-training setups. Additionally, we seek to expand DINO's capabilities by incorporating several modifications to its protocol and assess their impact on different network architectures. Notably, we found that incorporating a temperature parameter in DINO leads to superior results on the ImageNet dataset, especially when combined with experience replay. Our analysis also highlights the potential issues with current self-supervised evaluation protocols and proposes potential improvements.

A new viscous fluid model of the universe has been developed and studied using the Friedmann equations, with a viscosity coefficient tied to the specific fluid coupled with a cosmological constant. This coupling results in a unique interaction between the fluid's viscosity and the cosmological constant, potentially eliminating the universe's acceleration and transition to a radiation-dominated phase. However, a de Sitter phase remains a possibility, and the model also exhibits a phase where the Hubble parameter's rate of change is zero. This study further explores the cosmological implications of the viscosity coefficient, including the possibility of mapping the model to a previously studied fluid model. Furthermore, the model's dynamics are examined using phase portraits in different epochs, and the compatibility with observations is assessed by numerically solving the field equation. This investigation provides a framework for the model's behavior and offers avenues for future research.

This study examines the incompressible Euler equations in higher-dimensional spaces,
specifically those above three dimensions. Our investigation focuses on the optimal
conditions for the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem in these spaces. We find that
the optimal conditions coincide with the non-existence of low-frequency bounds for
the initial data in these spaces. Notably, we prove that the total vorticity $|\omega|(x,
0)$ is a crucial factor for the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem in $H^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$
and $H^{3/2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$. Our results are also enhanced by proving that the
total vorticity $|\omega|(x, 0)$ is a Nash equilibrium in the 2D space, and that
it remains bounded for all time in the 3D space.

The Artist is a DALL-E based tool that allows people to create images using natural language. It operates as a browser-based interface for generating images, which can be controlled through a set of predefined commands. These commands are defined by the Artist's developers to optimize performance and produce desired results. Despite being challenging to use, the Artist offers an uncommon level of control over the image generation process. To simplify the experience, we're introducing Stable Artist, a tool that incorporates our Standardized Control System to streamline setting parameters and producing consistent images. Additionally, we've updated the interface to improve usability and efficiency, allowing artists to produce images at high resolution while reducing generation time. Our modifications enable the production of high-quality images with minimal training data, making the system more accessible to anyone who uses DALL-E. We've also released a user-friendly tutorial to aid new users in producing results similar to our reference images. Our goal is to facilitate collaboration and encourage developers to contribute to the project, ultimately making Stable Artist a community-driven platform. The code and tutorial are available at the provided links.

By integrating Bayesian methods with deep learning, researchers can evaluate the limitations of predictive models and quantify uncertainty in outcomes. This has far-reaching applications, as predicting time-to-event outcomes accurately is critical in medical research and identifying high-risk patients. To overcome the limitations of traditional Bayesian approaches with limited data and complex models, a new method uses a continuous distribution for model parameters and incorporates prior knowledge into network structure and node characteristics. This approach was tested using simulated data and real-world studies on breast cancer and kidney disease, allowing for the assessment of model fit and predictive capability. Furthermore, a new metric has been developed to identify areas where the model's predictions are less reliable.

A novel approach to setting limits on dark matter interacting with nucleons has been developed, taking into account LHCb's ability to detect massless particles at a particle collider. This analysis puts an upper cap on dark matter interacting with nucleons, factoring in dark matter's decay into invisible particles and considering multiple possible dark matter scenarios such as soliton-like dark matter and its spin-dependent interactions. It's found that limits on dark matter interacting with nucleons are more stringent when there's a dark matter particle that decays fully into dark photons, and the dark photons have a mass less than 10 MeV. Furthermore, it's observed that limits on dark matter interacting with nucleons can be improved by detecting an excess in frequency of neutrinos at IceCube.

Researchers have been trying to understand the nature of magnetic bright points, small magnetic flux concentrations visible on the solar surface, which play a significant role in solar coronal mass ejections and flux transport. To gain insight into their characteristics, a extensive study was conducted using big data sets, consisting of 12 years of continuous data from the Hinode SOPHIA instrument, comprising 11,705 hours of high-resolution $6302 \ \rm{ \AA}$ magnetograms. This remarkable collection of data allowed for a detailed analysis of magnetic bright points, yielding 37,657,000 poles, which provided valuable insights into the spatial and temporal patterns of these features. The findings revealed that magnetic bright points are primarily located in active regions, with only $5.8\%$ found in quiet regions. The study also found that these regions are saturated with the electrostatic counterpart of the $3^1S_1-1^1S_0$ transition in neutral iron, pointing to an atomic mechanism that makes the formation of magnetic bright points possible in a tenuous atmosphere.

Human eye movements while watching videos can be closely linked to actual visual perceptions and recognition abilities. To gain deeper insights into how humans interpret visual information, we are seeking the minimum amount of video content that would still allow average human viewers to accurately identify the key entities within the footage. To this end, we have developed a cutting-edge multi-task deep neural network that can both identify the main entities in a video and then generate a simplified, eye-tracking-friendly version of the content, all while maintaining the original video's core characteristics. Our trained model exceeded state-of-the-art competitors in recent human action and activity detection challenges, and our experiments showed that our approach could effectively compress video content while preserving essential human perception and recognition abilities. Furthermore, our eye-tracking-friendly videos were found to significantly improve the accuracy of human eye movement detection algorithms. To facilitate further research, we will provide our model and the compressed, eye-tracking-friendly videos we created on our website.

We investigate monopole physics in the $SO(N_c)$ Yang-Mills theory with semi-compactification scale $\Lambda_{SM}$, and demonstrate that the bound monopole ground state possesses an external magnetic field response similar to superconductors, whose pressure releases energy as the field increases. The ground state monopole density in the pure gauge limit is found to be proportional to the square of the magnetic field strength. Notably, the bound monopole ground state exhibits a transition from type-I to type-II superconductivity behavior as $N_c$ increases. Furthermore, the ground state monopole charge density and energy density are calculated in the pure gauge limit, and these expressions are found to be comparable to those in the $SU(N_c)$ theory with an ultra-heavy quark mass.

To assess the efficacy of weather forecasting models, it is crucial to pick the most suitable evaluation method. This study compares three typical methods of evaluating weather forecasting models against the true state, which are calculating the average error, examining the model's probability distribution, and assessing its skill score in relation to the Clayton copula. The analysis utilizes a large public weather dataset and reveals that normalizing the data can significantly impact the ranking of models against each other. Therefore, when choosing an evaluation method, particular attention should be paid to how the model's output is normalized or not.

We've investigated how different types of CP violation in three-Higgs-doublet models impact the mass spectrum of their dark matter candidates. Our analysis shows that if we select models where there is no CP violation in the gauge sector and the mass of one of the Higgs bosons is set at 125 GeV, the mass range for dark matter candidates varies significantly based on the type of CP violation considered. This effect is particularly pronounced in models where we have a weakly coupled dark matter candidate. Our findings also show that even with very constrained parameters, we can account for the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Ultimately, we determine that future experiments at high-energy colliders will be essential in differentiating between different CP violation types in three-Higgs-doublet models.

We first verify the PPT square conjecture for matrix spaces having dimensions of $d \times d$ or $d \times 2d$. Our proof relies heavily on a finding reported by Keck and Tainster which shows that certain square maps containing PPT entanglement must also be fully entangled. This new proof offers significant computational benefits compared to the previous approach taken by Nishimura and ono. The PPT square conjecture has also been proven for general, infinite dimensional space, provided that the Schatten class is $d+1$, or $\Sigma_{\tau \leq 1} \tau^d d\tau$.

The unique transport mechanisms used by neurons to transport large amounts of cargo over long distances have long been an area of interest, particularly due to the distinct structural features of microtubules in different cells. To investigate the connection between these features and transport efficiency, we developed a model that simulates axonal transport, incorporating characteristics of microtubube polarity, organization, and spatial distribution. Our study, which involved analyzing virtual microtubules with varying properties, revealed that transport efficiency is significantly influenced by the distribution patterns of microtubules, and transport using kinesin motor proteins is more efficient than that using dynein when axonal microtubules exhibit end-to-end polarization. Conversely, when there is no preferential distribution of microtubules, dynein-based transport is more efficient. These findings, which align with experimental observations, suggest that the dynamic organization of microtubules in neurons plays a crucial role in optimizing axonal transport.

Banking institutions undergo continuous, autonomous updates to their accounts,
rendering past transaction records invalid and limiting their use in training
machine learning models. This problem is particularly challenging for areas
subject to strict regulations such as anti-money laundering and cross-border
transactions, where the need for accurate transaction analysis remains. Our
research addresses this issue by creating a novel, constraint-based framework
for generating banking graphs that mimics real-world activity patterns. This
approach involves a graph model derived from practical considerations, along
with a graph generator using expert knowledge of financial transactions. Our
results show our method's efficacy in producing realistic banking graphs that
maintain data privacy and satisfy regulatory requirements, while also enabling
the development of training data for your machine learning model. To facilitate
future research, we make our source code available at
https://github.com/graphlearn/banking-graph-generator.

In the final stages of a binary system that interacts with another star, the process of a massive star undergoing a certain type of explosion ($^{56}$Ni-rich Type Ia) typically leads to the formation of an unusual nuclear star, known as an interacting double white dwarf system. When these stars interact, they cause the white dwarf to expand into a red giant, which in turn causes the system's orbital path to move closer to the star. As this happens, the star that is not the white dwarf grows in mass and eventually experiences a certain type of explosion ($^{56}$Ni-rich Type Ia) as well. However, as the system interacts, the star that is not the white dwarf may cause the white dwarf to experience a certain type of explosion (most likely a thermonuclear explosion) as well. Recent studies have shown that the star that is not the white dwarf may cause the white dwarf to experience a certain type of explosion (most likely a thermonuclear explosion) as well, which in turn means that the resulting black hole and neutron star are born with different masses. This difference in masses poses a significant challenge to our current understanding of how these stars form and interact, particularly when it comes to the formation of an accretion disc. As a result, we are introducing a new model to understand the formation of an accretion disc in systems that are made up of a black hole and a neutron star.
